claim: The human TMEM263 gene encodes a small protein of 116 amino acids with two predicted transmembrane helices.
source: The human TMEM263 gene encodes a small protein of 116 amino acids with two predicted transmembrane helices (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the manuscript text and Figure 1A showing the protein structure and sequence alignment.

claim: TMEM263 is highly conserved across vertebrate species, with fish, frog, chicken, and mouse orthologs sharing 73%, 77%, 90%, and 97% amino acid identity with human TMEM263, respectively.
source: It is highly conserved across vertebrate species, with the fish (Danio rerio), frog (Xenopus tropicalis), chicken (Gallus gallus), and mouse (Mus musculus) orthologs sharing 73, 77, 90, and 97% amino acid identity with the full-length human TMEM263.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In humans, the TMEM263 transcript is widely and variably expressed across tissues, with liver having the highest expression.
source: In humans, the TMEM263 transcript is widely and variably expressed across tissues (Figure 1B), with liver having the highest expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data from the Human Protein Atlas and GTEx datasets shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Human TMEM263 protein is approximately 20 kDa in size when expressed in mammalian HEK293 cells.
source: Human TMEM263 protein is ~20 kDa in size when expressed in mammalian HEK293 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TMEM263 is localized to the plasma membrane when expressed in HEK293 cells.
source: This analysis showed that TMEM263 is localized to the plasma membrane when expressed in HEK293 cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by surface biotinylation experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Tmem263 is not required for embryonic development.
source: The genotype distribution of 82 pups at postnatal day 1 (P1) largely conformed to the expected Mendelian ratio for wild-type (WT) (+/+), heterozygous (+/-), and KO (-/-) mice (Figure 2D), indicating that Tmem263 is not required for embryonic development.
evidence: The claim is supported by Mendelian ratio analysis of P1 pups shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Loss of Tmem263 did not affect suckling at P1, as the milk spot was clearly visible in Tmem263-KO pups.
source: Loss of Tmem263 did not affect suckling at P1, as the milk spot was clearly visible in Tmem263-KO pups (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observation of milk spots in P1 pups shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No gross anatomical abnormalities in the axial skeleton, appendages, and cartilage were noted in Tmem263-KO pups at P1.
source: No gross anatomical abnormalities in the axial skeleton, appendages, and cartilage were noted in Tmem263-KO pups at P1, indicating that Tmem263-KO mice were born normal (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Alcian blue and Alizarin red staining shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The birth weights of pups at P1 were not different between genotypes.
source: The birth weights of pups at P1 were also not different between genotypes (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements at P1 shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Tmem263 is not required for prenatal growth.
source: Together, these data indicate that Tmem263 is not required for embryonic development and prenatal growth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal birth weights and lack of developmental abnormalities at P1.

claim: From P1 to P14, the weights of Tmem263-KO pups were not different from WT controls.
source: From P1 to P14, the weights of Tmem263-KO pups were not different from WT controls (Figure 2G), indicating no deficit in growth trajectory within the first 2 weeks of life.
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements from P1 to P14 shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Before and around the time of weaning at P21, clear differences in body weight were noted in Tmem263-KO mice relative to WT and heterozygous controls.
source: However, before and around the time of weaning at P21 when mice started to experience an accelerated growth spurt, coincident with the initiation of GH action (Lupu et al., 2001), clear differences in body weight were noted in Tmem263-KO mice relative to WT (+/+) and heterozygous (+/-) controls (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements at P21 shown in Figure 2G and cited literature on GH action timing.

claim: By adulthood (8 weeks of age), a severe growth failure phenotype was apparent in the Tmem263-KO mice.
source: By adulthood (8 weeks of age), a severe growth failure phenotype was apparent in the Tmem263-KO mice (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison of adult mice shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Both male and female KO mice exhibited the same striking degree of dwarfism, with body weight and body length dramatically reduced relative to WT controls.
source: Both male and female KO mice exhibited the same striking degree of dwarfism, with body weight and body length dramatically reduced relative to WT controls (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight and length measurements shown in Figures 2I-K.

claim: Partial loss of Tmem263 did not result in haploid insufficiency, as the heterozygous mice were indistinguishable from WT littermates across all measured parameters.
source: Partial loss of Tmem263 did not result in haploid insufficiency, as the heterozygous (+/-) mice were indistinguishable from WT littermates across all measured parameters.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of heterozygous and WT mice across multiple measurements.

claim: Both male and female Tmem263-KO mice were fertile, as indicated by viable mouse litters derived from multiple independent matings between male and female KO mice.
source: Both male and female Tmem263-KO mice were fertile, as indicated by viable mouse litters derived from multiple independent matings between male (-/-) and female (-/-) mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by breeding experiments producing viable litters.

claim: Tmem263 is required for postnatal growth and its absence causes postnatal growth retardation.
source: Together, these data indicate that Tmem263 is required for postnatal growth and its absence causes postnatal growth retardation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the growth failure phenotype observed in KO mice.

claim: Adult Tmem263-KO mice had much shorter femoral bones compared to WT and heterozygous controls.
source: In accordance with postnatal growth failure, adult Tmem263-KO mice had much shorter femoral bones compared to WT and heterozygous controls (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microCT imaging and femur length measurements shown in Figures 3A-B.

claim: Tmem263-KO mice showed marked reduction in trabecular bone volume, trabecular number, trabecular bone thickness, cortical tissue area, and cortical thickness relative to WT and heterozygous mice.
source: Quantification of various bone parameters in the distal femur indicated a marked reduction in trabecular bone volume, trabecular number, trabecular bone thickness, cortical tissue area, and cortical thickness in Tmem263-KO relative to WT and heterozygous mice (Figure 3C–H, regions of interest [ROI] for both trabecular and cortical bone analysis were adjusted in proportion to the length of bone, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by microCT quantification shown in Figures 3C-H.

claim: Normalization of cortical tissue area and cortical thickness to femur length indicated that skeletal geometry was proportional to that in WT littermates.
source: However, normalization of cortical tissue area and cortical thickness to femur length indicated that skeletal geometry was proportional to that in WT littermates (Figure 3I–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by normalized bone measurements shown in Figures 3I-J.

claim: Tmem263-KO mice had a much thinner growth plate compared to WT mice.
source: Histological analysis revealed a much thinner growth plate in Tmem263-KO mice (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological images shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Examination of growth plate morphology in the proximal tibia revealed a reduction in total growth plate length that was secondary to reductions in proliferative zone length in Tmem263-KO mice relative to WT controls.
source: Examination of growth plate morphology in the proximal tibia revealed a reduction in total growth plate length that was secondary to reductions in proliferative zone length in Tmem263-KO mice relative to WT controls (Figure 3L–M).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of growth plate zones shown in Figures 3L-M.

claim: The hypertrophic zone length was not different between genotypes.
source: The hypertrophic zone length was not different between genotypes (Figure 3N).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of hypertrophic zone length shown in Figure 3N.

claim: Tmem263 deficiency severely affects postnatal skeletal growth and acquisition.
source: Together, these data indicate that Tmem263 deficiency severely affects postnatal skeletal growth and acquisition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the bone phenotype data presented.

claim: Tmem263-KO mice had a marginal, though not significant, increase in serum GH compared to WT controls.
source: Tmem263-KO mice had a marginal, though not significant, increase in serum GH compared to WT controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum GH measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Serum IGF-1, IGFBP3, and IGFALS levels were markedly lower in Tmem263-KO mice relative to WT controls.
source: However, serum IGF-1, IGFBP3, and IGF acid labile subunit (IGFALS) levels were markedly lower in Tmem263-KO mice relative to WT controls (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figures 4B-D.

claim: Serum insulin levels were significantly lower in KO female mice and trended lower in KO male mice relative to WT controls.
source: Serum insulin levels were significantly lower in KO female mice and trended lower in KO male mice relative to WT controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by insulin measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Random-fed blood glucose levels were significantly lower in Tmem263-KO mice.
source: Random-fed blood glucose levels, however, were significantly lower in Tmem263-KO mice (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The combination of lower insulin and blood glucose levels suggests enhanced insulin sensitivity.
source: The combination of lower insulin and blood glucose levels suggests enhanced insulin sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the insulin and glucose measurements.

claim: These clinical features are commonly seen in patients with GHR mutations.
source: These clinical features are also commonly seen in patients with GHR mutations (Savage et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on GHR mutations.

claim: Serum Ca2+ levels were reduced in Tmem263-KO mice.
source: While serum Ca2+ levels were reduced in Tmem263-KO mice, serum phosphate levels and the Ca2+/P ratio were not different between genotypes (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum calcium measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Serum phosphate levels and the Ca2+/P ratio were not different between genotypes.
source: While serum Ca2+ levels were reduced in Tmem263-KO mice, serum phosphate levels and the Ca2+/P ratio were not different between genotypes (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum phosphate measurements shown in Figures 4H-I.

claim: Low IGF-1, IGFBP3, and IGFALS levels likely contribute to growth retardation and skeletal dysplasia in Tmem263-KO mice.
source: Together, these data indicate that low IGF-1, IGFBP3, and IGFALS levels likely contribute to growth retardation and skeletal dysplasia in Tmem263-KO mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the serum measurements and phenotype observations.

claim: The expression of Ghr, Igf1, and Igfals transcripts was significantly reduced (~4-fold) in the liver of Tmem263-KO mice relative to WT controls.
source: Indeed, the expression of Ghr, Igf1, and Igfals (IGF binding protein acid labile subunit) transcripts was significantly reduced (~4-fold) in the liver of Tmem263-KO mice relative to WT controls (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The expression of Igfbp3 was not different between genotypes.
source: The expression of Igfbp3, however, was not different between genotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR measurements.

claim: The hepatic GHR protein level was greatly reduced in Tmem263-KO mice compared to WT controls.
source: Consistent with the mRNA data, the hepatic GHR protein level was similarly and greatly reduced in Tmem263-KO mice compared to WT controls (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figures 5C-D.

claim: WT male mice injected with GH showed a robust GH-stimulated phosphorylation of Jak2 and Stat5b.
source: In contrast, WT male mice injected with GH showed a robust GH-stimulated phosphorylation of Jak2 and Stat5b (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: GH injection elicited a greatly diminished response in Tmem263-KO mice, as indicated by much lower magnitude (~60–80% reduction) of Jak2 and Stat5b phosphorylation relative to WT controls.
source: Relative to WT controls, GH injection elicited a greatly diminished response in Tmem263-KO mice, as indicated by the much lower magnitude (~60–80% reduction) of Jak2 and Stat5b phosphorylation relative to WT controls (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot quantification shown in Figures 5F-G.

claim: Reduced hepatic GHR expression and GH insensitivity potentially contribute to growth failure and skeletal dysplasia seen in the Tmem263-KO animals.
source: Together, these data point to reduced hepatic GHR expression and GHI as potentially contributing to growth failure and skeletal dysplasia seen in the Tmem263-KO animals.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the GHR expression and signaling data.

claim: 8.6% of the liver transcriptome in Tmem263-KO male mice were significantly altered relative to WT controls, with 1547 protein-coding genes up-regulated and 862 protein-coding genes down-regulated.
source: Indeed, 8.6% of the liver transcriptome in Tmem263-KO male mice were significantly altered relative to WT controls, with 1547 protein-coding genes up-regulated and 862 protein-coding genes down-regulated (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Among the major classes of genes and pathways most affected by the loss of Tmem263 are those involved in lipid and steroid metabolism, detoxification process, and xenobiotic handling.
source: Among the major classes of genes and pathways most affected by the loss of Tmem263 are those that involved in lipid and steroid metabolism, detoxification process, and xenobiotic handling (Figure 6B); all of the affected genes and pathways are known to be markedly altered in male mice in which GH signaling is disrupted due to Stat5b deficiency or an altered GH secretory profile (i.e. loss of pulsatile release of GH) (Udy et al., 1997; Clodfelter et al., 2006; Holloway et al., 2007; Davey et al., 1999a; Holloway et al., 2006; Lau-Corona et al., 2017; Waxman et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B and citations to literature on GH signaling disruption.

claim: Cux2 was one of the most up-regulated genes in general and was the most up-regulated transcription factor gene in the liver of Tmem263-KO male mice.
source: Remarkably, Cux2 was one of the most up-regulated genes in general and was the most up-regulated transcription factor gene in the liver of Tmem263-KO male mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcription factor expression analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The expression of Bcl6, a male-bias transcription factor gene, was significantly down-regulated in the KO male liver.
source: The expression of Bcl6, a male-bias transcription factor gene, was also significantly down-regulated in the KO male liver (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcription factor expression analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: All the well-known GH-regulated male-bias genes (growth and metabolism, cytochrome P450, and major urinary protein) were dramatically suppressed due to greatly diminished GH signaling.
source: Consequently, all the well-known GH-regulated male-bias genes (growth and metabolism, cytochrome P450, and major urinary protein) were dramatically suppressed due to greatly diminished GH signaling, whereas the female-bias genes (e.g. distinct set of cytochrome P450) were concomitantly and markedly up-regulated due to Cux2 overexpression in the male KO liver (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression heat maps shown in Figures 6D-F.

claim: Female-bias genes were concomitantly and markedly up-regulated due to Cux2 overexpression in the male KO liver.
source: Consequently, all the well-known GH-regulated male-bias genes (growth and metabolism, cytochrome P450, and major urinary protein) were dramatically suppressed due to greatly diminished GH signaling, whereas the female-bias genes (e.g. distinct set of cytochrome P450) were concomitantly and markedly up-regulated due to Cux2 overexpression in the male KO liver (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression heat maps shown in Figures 6D-F.

claim: Tmem263-KO male mice down-regulate 110 genes considered to be male-specific and up-regulate 174 genes considered to be female-specific when compared to WT male vs female liver data.
source: When compared to WT male vs female liver data, Tmem263-KO male mice down-regulate 110 genes considered to be male-specific and up-regulate 174 genes considered to be female-specific (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 6G comparing to published datasets.

claim: Loss of Tmem263 results in a high degree of liver transcript feminization in the male mouse.
source: This indicates in the male mouse, loss of Tmem263 results in a high degree of liver transcript feminization, a phenomenon usually prevented by normal GH signaling in male liver (Lau-Corona et al., 2017; Waxman et al., 1991; Zhang et al., 2012; Waxman and O'Connor, 2006; Norstedt and Palmiter, 1984).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the gene expression overlap analysis and supported by citations to literature on GH signaling and sexual dimorphism.

claim: Tmem263-KO male liver displays 176 shared up-regulated genes and 128 shared down-regulated genes when compared to hypophysectomized male mouse liver.
source: When compared to the DEG list of hypophysectomized male mouse liver – which lacks pituitary hormones (including GH) due to surgical removal of the pituitary gland – Tmem263-KO male liver displays 176 shared up-regulated genes and 128 shared down-regulated genes (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 6H comparing to published datasets.

claim: Tmem263-KO male liver shares 78 up-regulated and 91 down-regulated DEGs with Stat5b-KO male liver.
source: We again observed a high degree of overlap between the two KO mouse models, as Tmem263-KO male liver shares 78 up-regulated and 91 down-regulated DEGs with Stat5b-KO male liver.
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis comparing to published Stat5b-KO data.

claim: The underlying cause of the severe growth retardation and skeletal dysplasia seen in Tmem263-KO mice is most likely attributed to disrupted GH signaling in the liver and possibly other organs such as the bone.
source: Altogether, these transcriptomic data provide supporting evidence that the underlying cause of the severe growth retardation and skeletal dysplasia seen in Tmem263-KO mice is most likely attributed to disrupted GH signaling in the liver and possibly other organs such as the bone (Figure 6J).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the transcriptomic data and summarized in Figure 6J.

claim: TMEM263 is a GWAS candidate gene associated with BMD.
source: TMEM263 is a GWAS candidate gene associated with BMD (Calabrese et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a GWAS study.

claim: Mice lacking Tmem263 showed severe postnatal growth failure and had dramatically reduced bone volume and growth plate length.
source: Mice lacking Tmem263 showed severe postnatal growth failure and had dramatically reduced bone volume and growth plate length.
evidence: The claim is supported by the phenotypic data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: This phenotype is likely due to a disrupted GH/IGF-1 axis stemming from hepatic GH insensitivity and low IGF-1 production.
source: This phenotype is likely due to a disrupted GH/IGF-1 axis stemming from hepatic GHI and low IGF-1 production.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data on GHR expression, signaling, and serum IGF-1 levels.

claim: This is the first study documenting the physiological function of TMEM263.
source: This is the first study documenting the physiological function of this enigmatic, but highly conserved, membrane protein.
evidence: The claim is stated by the authors based on the novelty of their findings.

claim: Defects in any component of the GH/IGF-1 axis leads to a variable severity of postnatal growth failure (short stature) and skeletal dysplasia in humans and animal models.
source: In humans and animal models, defects in any component of the GH/IGF-1 axis leads to a variable severity of postnatal growth failure (short stature) and skeletal dysplasia.
evidence: The claim is supported by extensive citations to literature on GH/IGF-1 axis components.

claim: Tmem263-KO mice exhibited phenotypes closely resembling Ghr and Igf1 KO mice and humans with GH insensitivity.
source: Interestingly, Tmem263-KO mice exhibited phenotypes closely resembling Ghr and Igf1 KO mice (Lupu et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 1997; Baker et al., 1993) and humans with GHI.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published mouse models and clinical literature.

claim: The main defect leading to the shortening of the growth plate in Tmem263-KO mice is decreased in the size of the proliferative zone, which was also reported in Ghr KO mice.
source: The main defect leading to the shortening of the growth plate in Tmem263-KO mice is decreased in the size of the proliferative zone, which was also reported in Ghr KO mice (Sims et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by the growth plate measurements and citation to Ghr KO literature.

claim: The dwarf Tmem263-KO mice had normal to marginally higher serum GH, but low IGF-1, IGFBP3, and IGFALS levels, which is also the case in Ghr KOs.
source: Moreover, the dwarf Tmem263-KO mice had normal to marginally higher serum GH, but low IGF-1, IGFBP3, and IGFALS levels, which is also the case in Ghr KOs (Zhou et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum measurements and citation to Ghr KO literature.

claim: In Tmem263-KO male mice, GH injection elicited a greatly muted JAK2/STAT5 signaling response relative to WT controls.
source: In Tmem263-KO male mice, GH injection elicited a greatly muted JAK2/STAT5 signaling response relative to WT controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis of phosphorylated JAK2 and STAT5.

claim: GH is known to play an important role in regulating sex-dependent gene expression in liver, and a deficit in GH action results in the feminization of the male liver transcriptome.
source: GH is known to play an important role in regulating sex-dependent gene expression in liver, and a deficit in GH action results in the feminization of the male liver transcriptome (Lau-Corona et al., 2017; Waxman et al., 1991; Zhang et al., 2012; Waxman and O'Connor, 2006; Norstedt and Palmiter, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on GH and sexual dimorphism.

claim: Due to reduced hepatic GH signaling, the liver gene expression profile of Tmem263-KO male mice resembled that of WT female, hypophysectomized male, and Stat5b-KO male mice.
source: Due to reduced hepatic GH signaling, the liver gene expression profile of Tmem263-KO male mice resembled that of WT female, hypophysectamized male, and Stat5b-KO male mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of transcriptomic data with published datasets.

claim: One explanation for GH insensitivity in Tmem263-KO mice is the striking reduction in hepatic Ghr protein level induced by the loss of Tmem263.
source: One explanation is the striking reduction in hepatic Ghr protein level induced by the loss of Tmem263.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the GHR protein measurements.

claim: The decrease in Ghr protein level reflects, at least in part, lower transcription of the Ghr gene.
source: Because we also observed reduced expression of hepatic Ghr transcript, the decrease in Ghr protein level reflects, at least in part, lower transcription of the Ghr gene.
evidence: The claim is inferred from both mRNA and protein measurements.

claim: How a deficiency in Tmem263, a putative plasma membrane protein, led to altered hepatic Ghr transcript and protein level is presently unknown.
source: How a deficiency in Tmem263, a putative plasma membrane protein, led to altered hepatic Ghr transcript and protein level is presently unknown, and is a major limitation of the current study.
evidence: The authors acknowledge this as an unknown mechanism and limitation.

claim: Tmem263 may play a posttranscriptional role in Ghr processing, stability, turnover, trafficking, and/or signaling.
source: We cannot, however, exclude the possibility that Tmem263 plays a posttranscriptional role in Ghr processing, stability, turnover, trafficking, and/or signaling.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging alternative mechanisms.

claim: Trafficking defect in GHR has been previously documented, where mutations located at the extracellular domain of the GHR failed to localize to the plasma membrane when expressed in cultured cells.
source: Trafficking defect in GHR has been previously documented, where mutations located at the extracellular domain of the GHR failed to localize to the plasma membrane when expressed in cultured cells (Duquesnoy et al., 1991; Maamra et al., 2006; Fang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on GHR trafficking defects.

claim: Both human and mouse TMEM263 and GHR are widely expressed across tissues, especially highly expressed in liver.
source: Since both human and mouse TMEM263 and GHR are widely expressed across tissues (Ballesteros et al., 2000), as well as being highly expressed in liver (especially in human), the loss of Tmem263 in the KO mice may have a disproportionate impact on hepatic Ghr function.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data and citation to literature.

claim: The loss of Tmem263 in the KO mice may have a disproportionate impact on hepatic Ghr function.
source: Since both human and mouse TMEM263 and GHR are widely expressed across tissues (Ballesteros et al., 2000), as well as being highly expressed in liver (especially in human), the loss of Tmem263 in the KO mice may have a disproportionate impact on hepatic Ghr function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on expression patterns.

claim: It is not known whether the dwarf chicken with a loss-of-function mutation in TMEM263 is also insensitive to GH stimulation.
source: It is not known whether the dwarf chicken with a loss-of-function mutation in TMEM263 is also insensitive to GH stimulation.
evidence: The authors acknowledge this as unknown.

claim: There is only one documented case of a loss-of-function mutation in TMEM263, and it was associated with severe skeletal dysplasia in a fetus.
source: To date, there is only one documented case of a loss-of-function mutation in TMEM263, and it was associated with severe skeletal dysplasia in a fetus (Mohajeri et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a case report.

claim: It is unclear whether the TMEM263 mutation in the fetus is compatible with postnatal survival and its impact on the severity of postnatal growth retardation.
source: Because pregnancy was terminated before full term, it is unclear whether this mutation is compatible with postnatal survival and its impact on the severity of postnatal growth retardation.
evidence: The authors acknowledge this as unknown due to pregnancy termination.

claim: Rare homozygous loss-of-function mutations and variants of TMEM263 may cause Laron-type dwarfism with characteristic GH insensitivity.
source: Nevertheless, it is tempting to speculate on the possibility that rare homozygous loss-of-function mutations and variants of TMEM263 may cause Laron-type dwarfism with characteristic GHI.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the mouse phenotype.

claim: Only one homozygous missense mutation in the TMEM263 gene has been discovered from over 141,000 aggregated human exomes and genomes sequenced.
source: Intriguingly, only one homozygous missense mutation in the TMEM263 gene has been discovered thus far from over 141,000 aggregated human exomes and genomes sequenced (Genome Aggregation Database; gnomAD v2.1.1) (Karczewski et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the gnomAD database.

claim: Rare heterozygous splice-site, frameshift, and nonsense mutations in the TMEM263 gene have been documented in the gnomAD database.
source: Rare heterozygous splice-site, frameshift, and nonsense mutations in the TMEM263 gene have also been documented in the gnomAD database (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the gnomAD database.

claim: The homozygous D17N missense mutation found in 40 individuals (allele frequency of 0.006795) may impact TMEM263 function and affect postnatal linear growth.
source: Since the Asp-17 residue is highly conserved from fish to man, we speculate that the homozygous D17N missense mutation found in 40 individuals (allele frequency of 0.006795) may impact TMEM263 function and affect postnatal linear growth.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on conservation of the residue.

claim: It would be of considerable interest to ascertain whether individuals with the D17N variant have short stature.
source: It would be of considerable interest to ascertain whether individuals with the D17N variant have short stature.
evidence: The authors suggest this as a future research direction.

claim: TMEM263 should be considered a potential candidate gene in screening children with idiopathic growth failure.
source: Since TMEM263 has not yet been associated with postnatal dwarfism in human, it should be considered a potential candidate gene in screening children with idiopathic growth failure.
evidence: The authors suggest this as a clinical implication of their findings.

claim: Single nucleotide polymorphisms in TMEM263 are associated with bone mineral density in humans.
source: Single nucleotide polymorphisms in TMEM263 are associated with bone mineral density in humans and mutations are associated with dwarfism in chicken and severe skeletal dysplasia in at least one human fetus.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by GWAS literature.

claim: Mutations in TMEM263 are associated with dwarfism in chicken.
source: Single nucleotide polymorphisms in TMEM263 are associated with bone mineral density in humans and mutations are associated with dwarfism in chicken and severe skeletal dysplasia in at least one human fetus.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to chicken genetics literature.

claim: Mutations in TMEM263 are associated with severe skeletal dysplasia in at least one human fetus.
source: Single nucleotide polymorphisms in TMEM263 are associated with bone mineral density in humans and mutations are associated with dwarfism in chicken and severe skeletal dysplasia in at least one human fetus.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to a case report.

claim: Deletion of the Tmem263 gene in mice causes severe postnatal growth failure, proportional dwarfism, and impaired skeletal acquisition.
source: Deletion of the Tmem263 gene in mice causes severe postnatal growth failure, proportional dwarfism, and impaired skeletal acquisition.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by phenotypic data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mice lacking Tmem263 show no differences in body weight within the first 2 weeks of postnatal life.
source: Mice lacking Tmem263 show no differences in body weight within the first 2 weeks of postnatal life.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by body weight measurements.

claim: By P21 there is a dramatic growth deficit in Tmem263-null mice due to a disrupted growth hormone (GH)/insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) axis.
source: However, by P21 there is a dramatic growth deficit due to a disrupted growth hormone (GH)/insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) axis, which is critical for longitudinal bone growth.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by body weight and hormonal measurements.

claim: The GH/IGF-1 axis is critical for longitudinal bone growth.
source: However, by P21 there is a dramatic growth deficit due to a disrupted growth hormone (GH)/insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) axis, which is critical for longitudinal bone growth.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tmem263-null mice have low circulating IGF-1 levels and pronounced reductions in bone mass and growth plate length.
source: Tmem263-null mice have low circulating IGF-1 levels and pronounced reductions in bone mass and growth plate length.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by serum measurements and bone phenotyping.

claim: The low serum IGF-1 in Tmem263-null mice is associated with reduced hepatic GH receptor (GHR) expression and GH-induced JAK2/STAT5 signaling.
source: The low serum IGF-1 in Tmem263-null mice is associated with reduced hepatic GH receptor (GHR) expression and GH-induced JAK2/STAT5 signaling.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by qPCR, immunoblot, and signaling assays.

claim: A deficit in GH signaling dramatically alters GH-regulated genes and feminizes the liver transcriptome of Tmem263-null male mice.
source: A deficit in GH signaling dramatically alters GH-regulated genes and feminizes the liver transcriptome of Tmem263-null male mice, with their expression profile resembling wild-type female, hypophysectomized male, and Stat5b-null male mice.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The liver expression profile of Tmem263-null male mice resembles wild-type female, hypophysectomized male, and Stat5b-null male mice.
source: A deficit in GH signaling dramatically alters GH-regulated genes and feminizes the liver transcriptome of Tmem263-null male mice, with their expression profile resembling wild-type female, hypophysectomized male, and Stat5b-null male mice.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by overlap analysis with published datasets.

claim: The data validates the causal role for Tmem263 in regulating postnatal growth.
source: Collectively, our data validates the causal role for Tmem263 in regulating postnatal growth and raises the possibility that rare mutations or variants of TMEM263 may potentially cause GH insensitivity and impair linear growth.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Rare mutations or variants of TMEM263 may potentially cause GH insensitivity and impair linear growth.
source: Collectively, our data validates the causal role for Tmem263 in regulating postnatal growth and raises the possibility that rare mutations or variants of TMEM263 may potentially cause GH insensitivity and impair linear growth.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a speculative conclusion.

claim: GWAS have identified a large number of potential genes associated with bone mineral density.
source: In exploring the heritability of bone growth and mass, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified a large number of potential genes associated with bone mineral density (BMD) (Estrada et al., 2012; Kemp et al., 2017), bone structure (Zhao et al., 2010; Styrkarsdottir et al., 2019), and height (Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: GWAS have identified a large number of potential genes associated with bone structure.
source: In exploring the heritability of bone growth and mass, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified a large number of potential genes associated with bone mineral density (BMD) (Estrada et al., 2012; Kemp et al., 2017), bone structure (Zhao et al., 2010; Styrkarsdottir et al., 2019), and height (Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: GWAS have identified a large number of potential genes associated with height.
source: In exploring the heritability of bone growth and mass, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified a large number of potential genes associated with bone mineral density (BMD) (Estrada et al., 2012; Kemp et al., 2017), bone structure (Zhao et al., 2010; Styrkarsdottir et al., 2019), and height (Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: It remains a daunting challenge to prioritize and establish the causal role for GWAS candidate genes.
source: However, it remains a daunting challenge to prioritize and establish the causal role for these candidate genes.
evidence: The claim reflects a known challenge in the field.

claim: Only a limited number of the GWAS candidate genes have been functionally validated to play a causal role.
source: Consequently, only a limited number of the GWAS candidate genes have been functionally validated to play a causal role.
evidence: The claim reflects the current state of the field.

claim: TMEM263 was identified through associations between femoral neck BMD and heel bone BMD.
source: TMEM263, also referred to as C12orf23, was identified through associations between femoral neck BMD and heel bone BMD (Estrada et al., 2012; Kemp et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: Gene network analysis placed TMEM263 in a module related to osteoblast function.
source: Its function is unknown, but subsequent gene network analysis placed TMEM263 in a module related to osteoblast function (Calabrese et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a gene network analysis study.

claim: A nonsense mutation (Trp59*) that truncates the TMEM263 protein is linked to dwarfism in chicken.
source: Intriguingly, a nonsense mutation (Trp59*) that truncates the TMEM263 protein is linked to dwarfism in chicken (Wu et al., 2018), although it is unclear if this mutation directly causes dwarfism.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a chicken genetics study.

claim: It is unclear if the Trp59* mutation in chicken directly causes dwarfism.
source: Intriguingly, a nonsense mutation (Trp59*) that truncates the TMEM263 protein is linked to dwarfism in chicken (Wu et al., 2018), although it is unclear if this mutation directly causes dwarfism.
evidence: The authors acknowledge uncertainty about causality in the chicken model.

claim: A two nucleotide deletion that causes a frameshift and premature termination in TMEM263 was implicated as a candidate gene for a severe case of autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia in a fetus.
source: More recently, a two nucleotide deletion that causes a frameshift and premature termination in TMEM263 was implicated as a candidate gene for a severe case of autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia in a fetus (Mohajeri et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a case report.

claim: Little is known about TMEM263 and its function.
source: Apart from this limited information, little is known about TMEM263 and its function.
evidence: The authors state this as background for their study.

claim: The growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) axis plays a critical and essential role in postnatal growth.
source: It is known that the growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) axis plays a critical and essential role in postnatal growth (David et al., 2011; Efstratiadis, 1998; Savage et al., 2011; Rosenfeld et al., 2007; Rosenfeld et al., 1994; Qian et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by extensive citations to literature on the GH/IGF-1 axis.

claim: Defect in any component of the GH/IGF-1 axis causes a variable spectrum (modest to severe) of growth retardation and skeletal dysplasia in humans and in animal models.
source: Defect in any component of this axis causes a variable spectrum (modest to severe) of growth retardation and skeletal dysplasia in humans and in animal models (Lupu et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 1997; Baker et al., 1993; Liu et al., 1993; Davey et al., 1999b; Kofoed et al., 2003; Udy et al., 1997; Hwa et al., 2007; Klammt et al., 2018; Godowski et al., 1989; Woods et al., 1996; Abuzzahab et al., 2003; Lanning and Carter-Su, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by extensive citations to literature on GH/IGF-1 axis defects.

claim: TMEM263 may be a novel regulator of the GH/IGF-1 axis.
source: Since mutation in TMEM263 is linked to human skeletal dysplasia and dwarfism in chicken, and TMEM263 is also a GWAS candidate gene for BMD, we speculated that TMEM263 may be a novel regulator of the GH/IGF-1 axis.
evidence: The authors state this as their hypothesis.

claim: Tmem263 is not required for fertility.
source: We showed here that Tmem263 is not required for embryonic development, prenatal growth, and fertility.
evidence: The claim is supported by successful breeding of KO mice.

claim: Mice lacking Tmem263 exhibit growth arrest and have severe reduction in bone mass and growth plate length.
source: However, mice lacking Tmem263 exhibit growth arrest and have severe reduction in bone mass and growth plate length.
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight, bone, and growth plate measurements.

claim: These defects are due to a marked reduction in GH receptor (Ghr) mRNA and protein expression in the liver.
source: We further showed that these defects are due to a marked reduction in GH receptor (Ghr) mRNA and protein expression in the liver.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR and immunoblot data.

claim: Reduced GHR expression resulted in greatly diminished GH-induced JAK2/STAT5 signaling critical for IGF-1 synthesis and secretion by the liver.
source: This resulted in greatly diminished GH-induced JAK2/STAT5 signaling critical for IGF-1 synthesis and secretion by the liver.
evidence: The claim is supported by signaling assays and is consistent with known GH signaling pathways.

claim: Tmem263 knockout mice had low circulating IGF-1 and IGF binding protein 3 (IGFBP3), leading to dramatic postnatal growth failure and skeletal dysplasia.
source: Consequently, Tmem263 knockout (KO) mice had low circulating IGF-1 and IGF binding protein 3 (IGFBP3), leading to dramatic postnatal growth failure and skeletal dysplasia.
evidence: The claim is supported by serum measurements and phenotypic observations.

claim: Loss-of-function studies have provided direct evidence that Tmem263 is a causal gene affecting BMD and postnatal growth.
source: Our loss-of-function studies have provided direct evidence that Tmem263 is a causal gene affecting BMD and postnatal growth, and it does so by regulating the GH/IGF-1 axis, specifically hepatic GHR protein levels.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Tmem263 regulates BMD and postnatal growth by regulating the GH/IGF-1 axis, specifically hepatic GHR protein levels.
source: Our loss-of-function studies have provided direct evidence that Tmem263 is a causal gene affecting BMD and postnatal growth, and it does so by regulating the GH/IGF-1 axis, specifically hepatic GHR protein levels.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The GH insensitivity phenotype seen in Tmem263-KO mice raises the possibility that rare TMEM263 mutations or variants may potentially disrupt postnatal linear growth due to deficiency in GHR signaling.
source: The GH insensitivity (GHI) phenotype seen in Tmem263-KO mice raises the intriguing possibility that rare TMEM263 mutations or variants may potentially disrupt postnatal linear growth due to deficiency in GHR signaling.
evidence: The claim is stated as a speculative conclusion from the study.

claim: The mouse Tmem263 is variably and widely expressed across tissues.
source: The mouse Tmem263 is also variably and widely expressed across tissues (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mouse Tmem263 gene consists of three exons, and exon 3 encodes ~81% of the full-length protein.
source: The mouse Tmem263 gene (NM_001013028) consists of three exons, and exon 3 encodes ~81% of the full-length protein.
evidence: The claim is based on gene structure analysis.

claim: Deletion of the Tmem263 gene resulted in complete absence of the transcript in liver and hypothalamus.
source: As expected, deletion of the Tmem263 gene resulted in complete absence of the transcript in liver and hypothalamus (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The organ weights (liver, pancreas, heart, kidney, spleen, gastrocnemius, and brain) of the KO mice were significantly lower relative to WT controls.
source: Due to their small size, the organ weights (liver, pancreas, heart, kidney, spleen, gastrocnemius, and brain) of the KO mice were also significantly lower relative to WT controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by organ weight measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When normalized to body weight, Tmem263-KO mice had lower relative weights of liver (male only), spleen (male only), and skeletal muscle (gastrocnemius) and higher kidney and brain weight.
source: When normalized to their body weight, Tmem263-KO mice also had lower relative weights of liver (male only), spleen (male only), and skeletal muscle (gastrocnemius) and higher kidney and brain weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by normalized organ weight measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The litter size from KO parents was ~30–40% smaller, though this observation was based only on a limited number of litters produced.
source: The litter size in general was ~30–40% smaller, though this observation was based only on a limited number of litters produced.
evidence: The claim is based on limited breeding observations.

claim: The smaller litter size might reflect potential constraints imposed by the size of the KO dam.
source: The smaller litter size might reflect potential constrains imposed by the size of the KO dam.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the small size of KO females.

claim: Mice born from homozygous KO parents appeared largely normal with no gross physical or behavioral abnormalities noted except their pronounced dwarfism.
source: Mice born from homozygous KO (-/-) parents appeared largely normal with no gross physical or behavioral abnormalities noted except their pronounced dwarfism.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of offspring from KO parents.

claim: A majority (~75%) of the circulating IGF-1 is secreted by the liver.
source: A majority (~75%) of the circulating IGF-1 is secreted by the liver (Ohlsson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on IGF-1 production.

claim: The GH/IGF-1 axis is likely disrupted at the liver in Tmem263-KO mice.
source: Because Tmem263-KO mice had normal to marginally higher GH but low IGF-1 and IGFBP3 levels, the GH/IGF-1 axis is likely disrupted at the liver.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the hormonal measurements.

claim: At baseline when mice were not injected with GH, there were no detectable phospho-Jak2 and phopho-Stat5b signals.
source: At baseline when mice were not injected with GH, there were no detectable phospho-Jak2 and phopho-Stat5b signals (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Impaired GH signaling results in widespread changes in the GH-regulated liver transcriptome of Tmem263-KO male mice.
source: Based on our current data and what is known in the literature (Clodfelter et al., 2006; Holloway et al., 2007), impaired GH signaling results in widespread changes in the GH-regulated liver transcriptome of Tmem263-KO male mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to literature.

claim: In male mice, when GH signaling or secretory profile is disrupted, the expression of male-bias genes is dramatically suppressed and the expression of female-bias genes are up-regulated due to their de-repression.
source: In male mice, when GH signaling or secretory profile is disrupted, the expression of male-bias genes is dramatically suppressed and, concomitantly, the expression of female-bias genes are up-regulated due to their de-repression in male mice (Lau-Corona et al., 2017; Waxman and O'Connor, 2006; Chia, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on GH and sexual dimorphism.

claim: This is thought to be the result of altered male-bias (e.g. Bcl6) and female-bias (e.g. Cux2) transcription factor expression that reciprocally regulates the hepatic expression of sex-bias genes in male and female mice.
source: This is thought to be the result of altered male-bias (e.g. Bcl6) and female-bias (e.g. Cux2) transcription factor expression that reciprocally regulates the hepatic expression of sex-bias genes in male and female mice (Conforto et al., 2012; Sugathan and Waxman, 2013; Meyer et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on transcription factors and sexual dimorphism.

claim: In male mice with disrupted GH signaling, Bcl6 expression is suppressed and Cux2 expression is markedly up-regulated, leading to transcriptional repression of male-bias genes and up-regulation of female-bias genes in the male liver.
source: In male mice with disrupted GH signaling, Bcl6 expression is suppressed and Cux2 expression is markedly up-regulated, leading to transcriptional repression of male-bias genes and up-regulation of female-bias genes in the male liver (Lau-Corona et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on GH signaling and transcription factors.

claim: The high overlap of liver DEGs between Tmem263-KO and hypophysectomized male mice suggests that Tmem263 deficiency disrupts GH action in the liver.
source: The high overlap of liver DEGs between Tmem263-KO and hypophysectomized male mice with a deficit in GH further suggests that Tmem263 deficiency disrupts GH action in the liver.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the overlap analysis with published datasets.

claim: Stat5b-KO male mice exhibit dwarfism and GH pulse resistance.
source: Lastly, Tmem263-KO male mouse liver DEGs were compared to those of Stat5b-KO male mice (Figure 6I), which exhibit dwarfism and GH pulse resistance (Udy et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on Stat5b-KO mice.

claim: The cardinal biochemical features of GH insensitivity states are low circulating IGF-1 and normal or increased GH levels.
source: In the clinical context, the cardinal biochemical features of GHI states are low circulating IGF-1 and normal or increased GH levels (David et al., 2011; Savage et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical literature on GH insensitivity.

claim: Failure of STAT5b to bind to the cytoplasmic tails of the GHR due to a truncation mutation leads to growth failure and a GH insensitivity state.
source: Failure of STAT5b to bind to the cytoplasmic tails of the GHR due to a truncation mutation also leads to growth failure and a GHI state (Milward et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on STAT5b mutations.

claim: Future mechanistic studies are needed to definitively establish the causal link between impaired GH/IGF-1 signaling and defect in skeletal acquisition and growth in Tmem263-KO mice.
source: However, future mechanistic studies are needed to definitively establish the causal link between impaired GH/IGF-1 signaling and defect in skeletal acquisition and growth in Tmem263-KO mice.
evidence: The authors acknowledge this as a limitation and future direction.

claim: Reduced transcription could decrease Ghr mRNA level, but other possible mechanisms could potentially contribute to the reduced Ghr transcript level as well, including altered mRNA splicing, polyA adenylation, mRNA export, and mRNA stability.
source: Although reduced transcription could decrease Ghr mRNA level, other possible mechanisms could potentially contribute to the reduced Ghr transcript level as well; these include altered mRNA splicing, polyA adenylation, mRNA export, and mRNA stability.
evidence: The authors acknowledge alternative mechanisms that could explain the reduced mRNA levels.

claim: Whether GHR mutations affect protein folding and/or a transport signal recognized by another protein has not been established.
source: Whether these mutations affect protein folding and/or a transport signal recognized by another protein has not been established.
evidence: The authors acknowledge this as unknown in the field.

claim: One important question to address is whether TMEM263 physically interacts with GHR along the secretory pathway or on the plasma membrane of hepatocytes.
source: One important question to address is whether TMEM263 physically interacts with GHR along the secretory pathway or on the plasma membrane of hepatocytes.
evidence: The authors suggest this as an important future research question.

claim: If physical association between TMEM263 and GHR exists, it might provide mechanistic insights into how TMEM263 regulates GHR function.
source: If such physical association exists, it might provide mechanistic insights into how TMEM263 regulates GHR function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a potential mechanism.

claim: The generation and characterization of Tmem263 cell-selective and tissue-specific KO mouse models will help unravel the impact of this protein across different organ systems.
source: The generation and characterization of Tmem263 cell-selective and tissue-specific KO mouse models will help unravel the impact of this protein across different organ systems.
evidence: The authors suggest this as a future research direction.
